llm_response.content:
EMPIRICAL RESEARCH PLAN  

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

1. Identification Strategy  
Method: Randomized‐encouragement instrumental‐variables design (2-stage least squares).

Rationale  
• Seats in oversubscribed non-guaranteed schools are allocated by lottery.  
• Within each priority group the draw is random, so a “win” provides exogenous variation in the probability of attending a preferred (and on average higher-quality) school.  
• Because some winners decline the seat and some losers subsequently transfer, “lottery win” is best used as an instrument (Z) for actual enrollment in a preferred school (D).  
• The design yields the causal effect of attending the school (Local Average Treatment Effect for compliers) on adult crime outcomes (Y).

The same framework can be extended to:  
(i) estimate ITT effects (βITT) using simple OLS of Y on Z, and  
(ii) explore mechanisms by interacting Z with baseline peer/school covariates or by a two-sample causal-mediation exercise.

2. Treatment and Control  
Treatment variable (D): Indicator that a student in fall 2002 actually enrolled in a school ranked higher on her submitted preference list than her guaranteed “home” school. We will measure quality by the school-level pre-period average test-score index; robustness: use value-added or suspension rate.  

Instrument (Z): Indicator that the student received a first-round lottery offer to her first-choice (or any higher-ranked) non-guaranteed school.  

Control group: Lottery applicants who did not receive an offer in the first round.  

Timing: Assignment occurs April 2002; treatment begins August 2002 (start of school year). Outcomes are measured over the 7 calendar years that follow (Aug 2002–July 2009).

3. Key Identifying Assumptions  
A1. Random assignment (Independence): Conditional on priority group × choice-option fixed effects, lottery wins are as-good-as random.  
– Plausible: CMS used centralized algorithm with publicly posted rules; we can verify by covariate balance tests.  

A2. First-stage relevance: Lottery win strongly increases probability of attending the preferred school.  
– Testable: Report F-stat > 10. CMS records show take-up ≥ 75 % for first-choice offers.  

A3. Exclusion restriction: Lottery win affects adult crime only through school attended (and consequential peers/quality), not through other channels (e.g., signaling to police).  
– Discussed below; we will bolster credibility by showing no effect on pre-period outcomes and by conditioning on distance-to-school to rule out trivial policing differences.  

A4. Monotonicity: No one is induced by winning to avoid attending the preferred school (no “defiers”).  
– Highly plausible—refusing a seat cannot force attendance.  

A5. SUTVA: One student’s lottery result does not directly affect another’s outcome except through their own treatment status.  
– Possible peer spillovers inside schools violate SUTVA, but by definition those spillovers are part of the treatment; cross-school general-equilibrium effects likely small in a 100-school district.

4. Threats to Identification & Mitigation  
T1. Non-compliance / attrition from CMS or Mecklenburg County (students move; later arrests occur elsewhere).  
Mitigation: (i) estimate ITT as policy-relevant lower bound; (ii) instrument for actual enrollment; (iii) use NC Department of Corrections data covering state-wide prison stays; (iv) show results robust to sample restricted to students continuously observed in CMS through 8th/11th grade.  

T2. Differential policing or geographic surveillance if winners attend schools in neighborhoods with different police intensity.  
Mitigation: Control for police-precinct fixed effects based on home address; perform robustness dropping “quality” moves that also drastically shorten home-to-school distance. Examine effects on arrests versus self-reported disciplinary records while in high school.  

T3. Data-linkage error (name/DOB) may be correlated with race or mobility.  
Mitigation: (i) restrict to unique name–DOB combinations; (ii) sensitivity analysis assigning unmatched observations worst-case arrest outcomes; (iii) compare match rates by lottery status—should be equal under randomization.  

5. R Code Outline  

```r
# 0. Packages
library(tidyverse)
library(fixest)          # fast OLS & IV
library(modelsummary)    # nice tables
library(sandwich)        # robust VCOV

# 1. Load data (paths are illustrative)
lottery   <- read_csv("cms_lottery_2002.csv")      # one row per applicant
schools   <- read_csv("school_characteristics.csv")# test scores, peers
crime     <- read_csv("adult_crime_2002_2009.csv") # arrests & incarceration

# 2. Merge & construct variables
data <- lottery %>%
  left_join(schools, by = c("offered_school_id" = "school_id")) %>%
  left_join(crime,  by = "student_id") %>%
  mutate(
    treat_attend = as.integer(enrolled_school_rank < home_school_rank),
    instrument   = offer_first_round,     # 1 = lottery win
    outcome_arrest = total_felony_arrests,# main outcome
    priority_fe = interaction(priority_group, choice_option),
    hs = (grade_2002 >= 9)
  )

# 3. Balance checks (pre-treatment covariates)
bal_vars <- c("female","black","hispanic","ell","frl",
              "baseline_math","baseline_reading","home_school_quality")
balance <- lapply(bal_vars, function(v){
  feols(as.formula(paste0(v, " ~ instrument")), data = data, se = "hc2")
})
modelsummary(balance, statistic = "conf.int", stars = TRUE)

# 4. First stage
fs <- feols(treat_attend ~ instrument | priority_fe , data = data, se = "hc2")
summary(fs)

# 5. Second stage (2SLS) – Main specification
iv_main <- feols(outcome_arrest ~ 1 | priority_fe | treat_attend ~ instrument,
                 data = data, se = "hc2")
etable(iv_main, se = "hc2")

# 6. Robustness: ITT, subgroup by baseline risk, add precinct FE
itt <- feols(outcome_arrest ~ instrument | priority_fe, data = data, se = "hc2")
sub_hi_risk <- data %>% filter(baseline_suspensions > 0)
iv_hr <- feols(outcome_arrest ~ 1 | priority_fe | treat_attend ~ instrument,
               data = sub_hi_risk, se = "hc2")

# 7. Sensitivity: Include police-precinct FE
iv_precinct <- feols(outcome_arrest ~ 1 | priority_fe + precinct_fe |
                     treat_attend ~ instrument,
                     data = data, se = "hc2")
```

6. Expected Results  
Theory suggests access to higher-quality schools and improved peer environments reduce future criminal activity via higher human-capital accumulation and socialization. I expect:  

• ITT: ≈ –0.05 to –0.08 felonies per person over 7 years (8–12 % decline off a baseline mean ≈ 0.6).  
• TOT (2SLS): ≈ –0.10 to –0.15 felonies per treated complier, translating to one felony averted for every 7–10 treated students.  
• Larger effects for males, minority youth, and those with prior suspensions; channels: mediating gains in 9th-grade math scores and reduction in high-school suspensions.

7. Validity Checklist (IV)  
C1: Instrument is strongly correlated with treatment  … 1  
C2: Instrument is as-good-as randomly assigned        … 1  
C3: Exclusion restriction holds                        … 0.5  
C4: Monotonicity                                       … 1  
C5: No interference/SUTVA                              … 0.5  

Total = 4/5.
